newsitem.title: USA: Hilton bid last resort to force ITT merger.
newsitem.headline: Hilton bid last resort to force ITT merger.

text.p: Hilton Hotels Corp's move to increase the price of its hostile takeover bid for rival ITT Corp could be Hilton's last shot at forcing ITT management to discuss a possible merger.

Financial analysts on Wednesday said preliminary analysis of the numbers shows a price above $70 could become dilutive to earnings. Moreover, they said in a conference call earlier, Hilton Chief Executive Officer Stephen Bollenbach stressed this offer is his company's final position.
"This is not the first volley in a negotiating scenario. If not this deal, then nothing," said Bruce Turner, analyst at Salomon Brothers.
Analysts said the $70 a share bid should be taken seriously because it matches the price ITT offered for 26 percent of its own shares when it announced its breakup strategy in July.
In making the higher offer, Hilton is hoping ITT shareholders will pressure ITT's board to put the offer up for a shareholder vote, analysts said.
Though a shareholder vote is not required, it is simply the fair thing to do, said David Wolfe, analyst at Oppenheimer & Co.
Earlier, Hilton raised its offer from a previous bid of $55 a share. That bid had been on the table since late January and had been roundly rejected by ITT.
An ITT spokesman has said the company's board would meet and review Hilton's higher bid.
If ITT again rejected the bid, which some analysts believe it will do, then Hilton's last resort is to hope the U.S. District Court in Nevada will force a shareholder vote.
Previous attempts in that court to force a vote, however, have been unsuccessful, and Turner said historically the courts have given a board wide latitude to determine its own course.
Meanwhile, analysts generally believed the $70 per share offer is a sound bid that would, as Hilton has said, be non-dilutive to earnings in 1998, the year when a merger would likely be completed.
"When I saw the $70 a share, it concerned me a little bit; but I've run the numbers and...I think it's a neutral deal in 1998," said Dennis Forst, analyst at McDonald & Co Investments.

Though many analysts had previously forecast that a figure above $65 a share would dilute Hilton earnings, they backed off that figure today. They noted many assumptions of the previous estimates have changed.
For instance, Hilton has said it may be able to achieve cost savings greater than the $100 million it had earlier forecast.
ITT's asset sales have changed earnings assumptions. Also, the stock prices have changed, which in turn affects the ratio at which Hilton would swap its shares for ITT's if a deal could be completed.
